answer.caveats: The cavity was modelled as an air-filled sphere 15 m across (radius 7.5 m) with its top at 40 m, so its centre is at about 47.5 m. Gravity: limestone density is about 2.6 g/cc, giving a density contrast of about -2.6 g/cc. The predicted peak is about -14 µGal against about 11 µGal of effective noise (S/N about 1.2), so the cavity is not detectable. Real limestone porosity and density could shift this somewhat. A larger, shallower, or upward-stoping cavity, or careful high-precision microgravity with repeated readings and good terrain and drift control, might raise S/N to marginal. Magnetics: limestone is nearly non-magnetic (k about 3e-4 SI), so the void's susceptibility contrast is tiny. The predicted anomalies (about 0.04 nT total field, about 0.002 nT vertical gradient) are far below the noise level. Magnetic fill or overlying sediments would not change this conclusion. Resistivity or ERT, seismic methods, or targeted drilling are better suited at this depth. Because the cavity is undetectable by all three methods, the recommended station spacing is 0 for each.

The cavity was modelled as an air-filled sphere 4 m across (radius 2 m) with its centre at 7 m depth. Gypsum density was taken as about 2.3 g/cm³, giving a density contrast of about -2.3 g/cm³. Gravity: the peak is about -10.5 µGal against an effective noise of 11.2 µGal (5 and 10 µGal in quadrature), so S/N is about 0.9. The anomaly width at half maximum would be about 10 m. Magnetics: gypsum is weakly diamagnetic (susceptibility about -1e-5 SI), so the cavity contrast is negligible. The total-field peak is about 0.006 nT and the gradiometer peak about 0.0002 nT, both orders of magnitude below the noise. The cavity size is assumed, not measured. A larger, shallower or elongated (tunnel-like) void, or a cluster of voids, would give a larger gravity signal. A void about 6 m or more across at this depth, or a microgravity survey with repeat readings, tight drift control and terrain corrections, could become marginal. Clay or water infill would reduce the contrast further. Better options for the top 5–10 m are electrical resistivity tomography, GPR (already showing fractures), seismic methods, or probe drilling.

The void was modelled as an air-filled sphere 10 m in diameter with its centre at 15 m depth, in limestone of density about 2.6 g/cc, giving a density contrast of about -2.6 g/cc. Gravity gives a negative peak of about -40 µGal against 11.2 µGal combined noise, so S/N is about 3.6 (marginal). The anomaly half-width (FWHM) is about 23 m, so stations every 4 m are recommended, preferably on a grid or several crossing profiles. Careful terrain, drift and tide corrections are needed. Limestone susceptibility is very low (about 3e-4 SI), so the void's magnetic contrast is tiny. The total-field anomaly is a few tenths of a nT and the vertical-gradient reading is about 0.06 nT, both far below field noise, so neither magnetic method is useful. The gravity estimate could change in several ways: - A water- or sediment-filled void would give a smaller anomaly. - A more elongated or larger cavity, or a surrounding loosened (low-density) zone, would give a larger anomaly. - Gravity effects from nearby open sinkholes and fissures need to be modelled. - Shallow karst heterogeneity may add geological noise above the instrument noise. Combining gravity with ERT or GPR would help.

The pocket was modelled as a sphere of radius 3 m with its centre at 11 m depth. Gravity peak is in µGal; the magnetic and gradient peaks are in nT. Gravity: textbook densities of about 2.0 g/cc for wet clay and 2.3 g/cc for gypsum give a contrast of about -0.3 g/cc. The predicted low is about 1.9 µGal against about 11 µGal of noise, so S/N is about 0.2. Magnetics: clay is weakly magnetic (about 2e-4 SI) and gypsum is slightly diamagnetic, giving a contrast of about 2e-4 SI. The total-field peak is about 0.1 nT against 2 nT of noise. The gradiometer peak is about 0.025 nT against about 0.5 nT of noise. None of the three methods would detect this target at this depth and size. The densities, susceptibilities and geometry are assumed values: clay with magnetite-rich alluvium, or an air- or water-filled void (contrast down to -2.3 g/cc), would give a stronger response. Even an air-filled void of this size would only reach about 14 µGal, which is still marginal at best. For this target, consider ERT, GPR (if the gypsum is not too conductive) or seismic methods instead.

The cavity was modelled as a sphere 2 m in radius with its centre about 7 m deep. Gravity: gypsum density was taken as about 2.3 g/cc and water as 1.0 g/cc, a contrast of about -1.3 g/cc. This gives a peak of about -6 µGal against about 11 µGal of noise, so S/N is about 0.5. Water filling cuts the anomaly to about 60% of the air-filled case. If the void is a long tunnel-like (2D) feature rather than a compact one, the peak rises to about 30 µGal, which would be marginal at 2-3 m spacing. Magnetics: gypsum is weakly diamagnetic (about -1e-5 SI) and water is about -9e-6 SI. The susceptibility contrast is therefore only about 4e-6 SI. The resulting anomalies are around 0.001-0.002 nT, far below both the total-field and gradiometer noise. Recommendation: none of the three methods will reliably detect this target. A microgravity survey with very low noise (about 3-5 µGal, repeat readings, careful terrain and drift control) might at best give a marginal result. ERT or GPR (if conductivity allows) would be better choices. Real voids may be larger, collapsed or connected to other voids, which could change these conclusions.

Gravity: modelled as a 30 x 30 m prism from 2 to 6 m depth, with textbook densities of soil 1.92 g/cc and clay 2.21 g/cc (contrast -0.29 g/cc). This gives a peak of about -37 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise, so S/N is about 3.3 (marginal). The anomaly FWHM is about 30-35 m, so stations at 5-6 m or closer are needed. Gravity needs careful terrain and height corrections: depression relief of a few metres alone gives free-air/Bouguer effects of tens of µGal, so precise levelling (DGPS, cm-level) is essential. Magnetics: the susceptibility contrast between loosened soil and clay is small and poorly constrained; about 4e-4 SI was assumed, giving roughly 1-1.5 nT total field and about 0.1 nT gradient, both below field noise. If the loosened zone is more strongly magnetic, or the soil is enriched in magnetic minerals, the magnetic methods could improve somewhat, but still not reliably. Real loosening may produce a smaller density contrast than the table values; if the contrast is only about 0.1-0.15 g/cc, gravity becomes undetectable. Consider ERT or GPR as complementary methods.

The cave was modelled as an air-filled sphere 2.5 m in radius, centred at 12.5 m depth. Gravity used a density contrast of about -2.6 g/cc (air against limestone at about 2.6 g/cc). This gives a peak of about -7 µGal, a half-maximum width of about 20 m, and S/N of about 0.65 against roughly 11 µGal of effective noise. Magnetics used a susceptibility contrast of about -3e-4 SI, since limestone is only weakly magnetic. That gives about 0.06 nT for total field (S/N about 0.03) and about 0.015 nT for the gradiometer (S/N about 0.03), so neither magnetic method can see an air void. Because no method passes, station spacing is given as 0. If the cave is larger, elongated as a gallery (2D cylinder geometry roughly doubles to triples the anomaly), shallower than 10 m, or part of a cluster of voids, the gravity signal could rise into the marginal range. In that case use 3-4 m stations with careful terrain, tidal and drift corrections and repeat readings. A clay- or terra-rossa-filled cave could give a weak magnetic signal. For this target, ERT or GPR are better complementary choices.

The passage was modelled as an infinite horizontal cylinder of air (radius 1.5 m, axis at 7.5 m depth) in gypsum of about 2.30 g/cm3. That gives a density contrast of about -2.3 g/cm3 and a peak gravity anomaly of about -29 µGal. The effective noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 2.6, which is marginal. The anomaly's full width at half maximum is about 15 m, so stations should be at most 3 m apart along profiles crossing the expected passage trend. Results need careful terrain and Bouguer reduction, repeat readings and drift control. Any loss of length, a smaller passage or partial sediment or water fill would push the anomaly below detection; several stacked passages could increase it. Gypsum is weakly diamagnetic (about -1e-5 SI), so the air-gypsum susceptibility contrast is negligible. The total-field anomaly is only about 0.02 nT and the vertical-gradient anomaly about 0.005 nT, far below field noise, so neither magnetic method will detect the cave regardless of strike direction. A magnetic response would only appear if the cave holds magnetic sediment fill, or if the cover contains clay or iron-oxide material contrasting with clean gypsum. Consider ERT or GPR as complementary methods.

The network was modelled as one infinite horizontal air-filled cylinder: radius 1.5 m, axis at 9.5 m depth, density contrast about -2.6 g/cm3 against limestone, and susceptibility contrast about -3e-4 SI. Gravity: the peak is about -26 µGal against 11.2 µGal effective noise, so S/N is about 2.3 (marginal). The FWHM is about 19 m (2z), giving station spacing of about 4 m, so the existing 5 m grid is borderline. Careful terrain, tidal and drift corrections are needed, and microgravity procedure is advised (repeat readings, base loops). A larger or shallower real network, or overlying low-density weathered or clay-filled zones, could increase the signal. Air- or water-filled voids would give a slightly smaller signal if partly sediment-filled; clay infill would reduce the contrast further. Magnetic and gradiometer surveys: limestone is nearly non-magnetic, so a void produces only about 0.2 nT (total field) and about 0.03 nT (gradient), far below noise. Magnetics would only help if the cavities contain magnetic clay or terra rossa infill. The anomaly amplitudes depend on the assumed limestone density and susceptibility and on passage strike. A 3D, discontinuous network would give smaller, more localised gravity anomalies than this 2D estimate. Complementary ERT or GPR (GPR depth is limited if clay is present) and drilling verification are recommended.

Gravity model: a 15 x 15 m prism from 5 to 12 m depth, using textbook densities (limestone about 2.55, clay about 2.21 g/cc, contrast about -0.34 g/cc). This gives a peak of about -30 µGal over the centre, with a full width at half maximum of about 20 m. Effective noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 2.7 (marginal). If the fill is softer, wetter or partly air- or water-filled, or the limestone is denser (contrast -0.5 to -0.7 g/cc), the anomaly could rise to 45-60 µGal. Clay against limestone gives a very small susceptibility contrast (about 1e-4 SI). At inclination -8.9° the induced total-field anomaly is a fraction of a nT, and the gradiometer signal is a few hundredths of a nT. Both are well below field noise. Microgravity is only usable with careful practice: repeat or base readings for drift, precise levelling (±1 cm), and terrain and building corrections. A dense grid at about 3-4 m is advised, ideally with borehole verification. Pinnacled karst bedrock, variable overburden and nearby structures can produce anomalies of similar size. Results depend on the assumed depth and fill material.

The target was modelled as a vertical cylinder 100 m across, with its top at 2 m and base at 40 m. Clay fill was taken as about 2.0 g/cm3 against gypsum at about 2.3 g/cm3, a contrast of about -0.3 g/cm3. This gives a gravity low of about -0.30 mGal (300 µGal) over the centre. Against about 11 µGal effective noise that is S/N of about 27, with a FWHM of about 100 m, so 20 m stations are enough (10 m if you want to define the edges). The peak gravity value is in mGal; the magnetic and gradient values are in nT. Magnetics assume a susceptibility contrast of only about 3e-4 SI (weakly magnetic clay against diamagnetic gypsum). That gives about 3.5 nT total field, S/N under 2. It would become marginal if the clay is more magnetic, for example iron-oxide-rich terra rossa. The gradiometer responds mainly at the doline edges, giving well under 1 nT, so it is not detectable. Several factors could change the gravity result: - Actual fill density and degree of compaction are uncertain; a smaller contrast or shallower fill would scale the anomaly down roughly in proportion. - Gypsum dissolution voids, anhydrite (about 2.9 g/cm3) at depth, and nearby dolines would all distort the signal. - Topographic depressions over the dolines need terrain and Bouguer corrections and precise levelling. Achieving 1 cm elevation accuracy (about 3 µGal) is essential.

The shaft was modelled as a vertical cylinder 1.5 m in radius, from 4 m to 40 m depth. Gravity: gravel fill (about 2.0 g/cc) in sandstone (about 2.35 g/cc) gives a density contrast of about -0.35 g/cc. The on-axis anomaly is about -3.6 µGal against about 11 µGal noise, so S/N is about 0.3. Magnetics: the susceptibility contrast between gravel and sandstone is near zero (assumed |Δk| ≤ 4e-4 SI). Total field: about 0.5 nT against 2 nT noise. Gradient: about 0.2 nT against 0.5 nT noise. Neither magnetic method is detectable. Several factors could make the target easier to find than this model suggests: (1) a real open void in a partially filled shaft (contrast about -2.35 g/cc for the void part) could give tens of µGal, consistent with the site's microgravity experience; (2) ferrous debris, a brick lining or capping could give strong magnetic anomalies; (3) collapse zones or a wider disturbed zone around the shaft would raise the gravity signal. If a void is suspected, a microgravity grid at about 1 m spacing is advised. The dimensions and properties used here are assumed.

Gravity was modelled as an air-filled vertical cylinder (radius 1.5 m, top 3 m, base 30 m) in sandstone with a density contrast of about -2.35 g/cc. This gives about -31 µGal on the shaft axis, with a full width at half maximum of about 9 m. Against 11.2 µGal combined noise that is S/N ≈ 2.8, so marginal. Detection would need dense stations at about 2 m or less, repeat readings, careful terrain and drift corrections, and precise elevations, because 1 cm of height error is about 3 µGal. If the shaft is partly backfilled or collapsed, or the sediment cover is thicker, the anomaly shrinks quickly. The magnetic estimates assume sandstone susceptibility of about 4e-4 SI with induced magnetisation only. The air void then gives under 1 nT total field and about 0.4 nT gradient, both below noise. Magnetics could still work indirectly if the shaft holds steel (rails, casing, cables, rubble with iron), which would give strong dipolar anomalies. A gradiometer is then the best reconnaissance tool and should be run at 0.5 m line spacing. GPR or ERT/microgravity could complement the survey, and the assumed shaft dimensions should be verified.

Model: the gallery is treated as an infinite horizontal cylinder of radius 1.25 m with its centre at 11.25 m depth. Gravity uses an air-granite density contrast of about -2.67 g/cm3, giving a peak of about -15.5 µGal. The effective gravity noise is about 11.2 µGal, so S/N is about 1.4, below the detection threshold. A low-noise repeat survey with stacked readings and careful terrain and drift corrections might bring it into the marginal range. Magnetics assume a granite susceptibility of about 0.0025 SI with induced magnetisation only, which is uncertain; the value is typical but very variable, and gallery strike relative to the field changes both shape and amplitude. Total field peaks below 1 nT against 2 nT noise. The gradiometer peaks at about 0.1 nT against 0.5 nT noise. Neither is detectable, and the void itself is magnetically weak. Gravity remains the most promising method if the gallery is shallower, larger, or has collapse or stope zones. The real anomaly could be larger if there are rails, steel supports or other metal debris, or a broader zone of disturbed ground. The 2D model overestimates the anomaly if the gallery is short or oblique to the line. Consider GPR or ERT as alternatives.

The shaft was modelled as an air-filled vertical cylinder (radius 1.6 m, top 1 m, base 18 m) in granite. For gravity I used a density contrast of -2.65 g/cc. The on-axis anomaly is about -91 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise, so S/N is about 8 and the half-maximum width is about 6 m. A 3.2 m square section would give slightly more, about -100 µGal. For magnetics I assumed the textbook granite susceptibility of 0.0025 SI, so the shaft is a contrast of -0.0025 SI, with induced magnetisation only in a 50975 nT field at 65.8 deg inclination. The magnetic results are only as reliable as that assumed susceptibility. Total field gives about -17 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 8, width about 4-5 m). The gradiometer gives about -11 nT against 0.5 nT noise (S/N about 20, width about 3-4 m). The gneissic host of the New Jersey Highlands is commonly far more magnetic and very heterogeneous. Magnetite ore bands, mine waste, backfill, collar timbers or steel will produce strong anomalies that could mask or mimic the void. The gradiometer is the fast screening tool; gravity responds directly to the void and is the more unambiguous confirmation, so follow up any target with gravity at about 1 m spacing (with terrain and building corrections) and then drilling. Any partial infill, water or a collapsed cap would reduce all of the anomalies. The site is a safety hazard: do not occupy ground over a suspected open shaft without first confirming it is stable.

The gallery was modelled as an infinite horizontal air-filled cylinder: radius 1.5 m, axis at about 26.5 m depth, in shale. Gravity: density contrast about -2.4 g/cc gives a peak of about -8.5 µGal. Effective noise is about 11.2 µGal, so S/N is about 0.8 and the void is not detectable. The anomaly would be about 53 m wide at half maximum, so about 10 m spacing would be used if it were detectable. Magnetics: shale susceptibility of about 6e-4 SI gives a contrast of about -6e-4 SI. That produces only about 0.05 nT in total field and about 0.004 nT in vertical gradient, far below field noise. Results would change if the void has collapsed and migrated upward, if there is a wider zone of goaf or broken rock, or if many parallel galleries add together. A collapse could raise the density deficit; multiple galleries or a broad goaf could raise the anomaly to marginal microgravity levels. Mine plans, boreholes, or seismic or deep resistivity methods are better suited to this depth-to-size ratio of about 9.

The shaft was modelled as an air-filled vertical cylinder, 1.6 m in radius, with its top at 8 m and its base at 30 m, in granite. Gravity: a density contrast of about -2.67 g/cc gives roughly -13 µGal on the shaft axis. Against an effective noise of about 11 µGal, S/N is about 1.2. Total-field magnetics: the shaft is a 'missing' induced magnetisation using a typical granite susceptibility of about 0.0025 SI. The top-pole approximation, with I = 65.8° and F = 50975 nT, gives about -0.85 nT. Against 2 nT of noise, S/N is about 0.4. Gradiometer: the response is about 0.19 nT against 0.51 nT of noise, so S/N is about 0.4. Granite susceptibility varies widely, from about 0 to 0.05 SI. A strongly magnetic granite (0.03 SI or more) could make the total-field response marginal. If the shaft is partly or wholly backfilled rather than open, the gravity contrast will be lower. A ferrous cap, rails or steel debris in the shaft could produce a much larger magnetic anomaly than this void-only model. The 8 m burial depth is assumed. At that depth, none of the three methods is expected to resolve the shaft, so electrical resistivity tomography, GPR or targeted drilling may be more suitable.

Gravity: the tunnel was modelled as an infinite horizontal cylinder (radius 1 m, centre 12 m deep). Using sandstone at about 2.35 g/cc against air gives a density contrast of about -2.35 g/cc. The peak is about -8 µGal. Effective noise is about 11.2 µGal, so S/N is about 0.7. If the host were denser (around 2.6 g/cc) the peak would be about -9 µGal, which is still below the noise. Magnetics: the air void is a weak negative susceptibility contrast against a typical sandstone (about 4e-4 SI). This gives peaks of order 0.06 nT for total field and about 0.01 nT for the gradiometer. Both are far below the field noise, regardless of the tunnel's strike relative to magnetic north. Answer: none of the three methods would detect this tunnel with standard equipment. A tunnel that is shallower, larger, metal-lined or contains services could change this. Microgravity with very careful repeat readings and terrain/building corrections, or seismic or ERT methods, might be considered, but the depth-to-size ratio (about 12:1) is unfavourable. The host properties are assumed from a vendor case study.

The tunnel was modelled as a 2D horizontal cylinder of radius 0.75 m with its axis at 8.75 m depth. For gravity, an air void in gravel of about 2.0 g/cc (contrast -2.0 g/cc) gives a peak of about -5.4 µGal. Against 11.2 µGal effective noise (5 and 10 µGal in quadrature), S/N is about 0.5. The anomaly's full width at half maximum would be about 17 m, so 3-4 m spacing would be needed if the anomaly were detectable. For magnetics, gravel susceptibility was taken as about 5e-4 SI, with air at 0. This gives sub-nT anomalies: about 0.16 nT for total field and about 0.03 nT for the gradiometer. Both are far below the noise of 2 nT and 0.5 nT respectively. The magnetic values assume a favourable strike and would be smaller for other orientations. All results are sensitive to the assumed tunnel size, depth and density. A larger or shallower cavity, a collapsed or wider gallery, or loosened ground around the tunnel could raise the gravity signal. Vertical access shafts are a much easier target to find. If the tunnel is water-filled, the density contrast falls to about -1.0 g/cc and the signal halves. Consider GPR, ERT or seismic methods, or locating the shafts first.

The chamber was modelled as an air-filled sphere 3 m in radius with its centre about 9 m deep. Assumed contrasts were a density of -1.9 g/cc (air against soil) and a susceptibility of about -1e-3 SI (air against typical soil); induced magnetisation only. Gravity gives about -18 µGal against 11 µGal of combined noise, so S/N is about 1.6. Total-field magnetics gives about 1 nT against 2 nT of noise. The gradiometer gives about 0.3 nT against 0.5 nT of noise. A box-shaped or larger void, including the passage and side recesses, could roughly double the gravity anomaly into the marginal range. Microgravity with careful terrain correction for the mound's topography would then be the best option, at about 2-3 m spacing over an anomaly roughly 14 m wide (FWHM). Mound topography, the stone kerb and the orthostats, and variations in the mound fill would also strongly affect real data.

Modelled as an air-filled infinite horizontal cylinder (radius 3 m, axis at 18 m depth) in clay with an assumed density of about 2.0 g/cm3, giving a contrast of about -2.0 g/cm3. Peak gravity is about -42 µGal against 11.2 µGal combined noise, so S/N is about 3.7 (marginal). The FWHM is about 36 m, so stations every 7 m or closer, on a profile laid perpendicular to the tunnel axis. The concrete or cast-iron lining is not modelled. Its added mass reduces the negative anomaly, and ignoring it gave about 20 % depth error, so the real gravity signal is probably weaker and may fall below the detection threshold. Careful terrain, building and basement corrections are needed in urban London, and cultural noise (traffic, nearby structures) may exceed 10 µGal. Magnetics assumed a clay susceptibility of about 1e-4 SI and induced magnetisation only. The air void then gives only about 0.06 nT total-field and less than 0.01 nT gradient, far below noise. A cast-iron or reinforced-steel lining could produce a strong magnetic anomaly, but urban magnetic clutter would likely mask it. Tunnel size, depth and orientation are assumed.

These are estimates from a 2D forward model: an air-filled 3 m x 2 m rectangular void with its top at 2.25 m, base at 4.25 m and centre at 3.25 m, treated as infinitely long because 40 m is much greater than its depth and assuming profiles run across the tunnel. Gravity: density contrast taken as -2.6 g/cc (limestone 2.6, air about 0), giving about -61 µGal against about 11 µGal noise, so S/N is about 5.5. That is only just above the clear-detection threshold. The FWHM is about 7 m, so use 1 m spacing. A limestone density of 2.4-2.5, as karstic or porous rock can have, or a tunnel that is partly backfilled or water-filled, would push the result into the marginal range. Terrain and building corrections and careful drift and tide control are needed. Magnetics: limestone is nearly non-magnetic (k about 3e-4 SI assumed). The void gives a total-field anomaly under 1 nT against 2 nT noise, and a gradiometer signal of about 0.45 nT against about 0.5 nT noise, so neither magnetic method would detect it. The exception would be tunnel infrastructure such as steel rails, pipes, rebar or lining, which could produce a much larger magnetic anomaly. Microgravity, possibly complemented by GPR or ERT, is the recommended approach. Use a surface hatch to calibrate the profile location.

The tunnel was modelled as an infinite horizontal air-filled cylinder in sandstone: radius 1.75 m, axis depth 5.75 m, density contrast about -2.35 g/cc. Gravity gives a peak of about -52 µGal against about 11.2 µGal combined noise, so S/N is about 4.7 (marginal). The anomaly's half-maximum width is about 11.5 m, so stations at 1-2 m spacing are suggested. The magnetic estimates assume a sandstone susceptibility of about 0.0004 SI and induced magnetisation only, with the tunnel strike taken as most favourable. The total-field anomaly is under 1 nT and the gradient anomaly is about 0.2 nT, both below field noise. The gravity S/N is close to the clearly detectable threshold, so it could change materially if the tunnel is shallower or larger, or if the sandstone is denser or more porous. It also depends on whether the tunnel is lined, partly backfilled or water-filled, since backfill or water would weaken the anomaly. Urban sites add noise from traffic, buildings, cellars and services, so terrain and building corrections and repeat readings will be needed. Steel services and rubble would dominate any magnetic data.

The room was modelled as a 5 x 5 m air-filled prism from 10 to 13 m depth (75 m³). Gravity: with a density contrast of -1700 kg/m³ the missing mass is about 1.3e5 kg. A point-mass approximation at 11.5 m depth gives a peak of about -6.4 µGal. The effective noise is about 11.2 µGal (5 and 10 µGal in quadrature), so S/N is about 0.6. Magnetics: I assumed a host susceptibility contrast of about -0.001 SI, since none was given. Treating the void as a dipole gives about -0.3 nT total field against 2 nT noise (S/N about 0.15). The gradiometer gives about -0.08 nT against about 0.5 nT noise (S/N about 0.15). None of the three methods would detect the room. Detection would become more plausible in these cases: a larger room, or connected tunnels and galleries; a shallower top; or a high-precision microgravity survey with dense repeat readings and careful terrain and building corrections. A more strongly magnetic tuff would raise the magnetic signal. GPR or ERT and seismic methods may suit better, though their 10 m depth reach in tuff is limited. The room dimensions and the tuff density are assumptions.

Model: an air-filled rectangular prism, 4 x 6 m in plan, from 1 to 3.5 m depth, in clay of density about 2.0 g/cm3, giving a density contrast of about -2.0 g/cm3. Gravity: the peak is about -80 µGal over the centre of the void. Effective noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 7 (clearly detectable). The anomaly width at half maximum is roughly 5-6 m, so 1 m station spacing on a grid is advised. Magnetics: assuming clay susceptibility of about 2e-4 SI, the void contrast is small, a few tenths to about 1.5 nT. The total-field estimate is about 1.5 nT against 2 nT field noise. The gradiometer estimate is about 0.7 nT against about 0.5 nT noise, so S/N is about 1.3. Neither magnetic method is reliable. Inside a church, magnetic surveys are further compromised by steel, heating pipes, wiring and the walls. Gravity readings need corrections for terrain and building mass: walls, pillars and altars produce gravity effects of tens of µGal. Floor-height variations need precise levelling to about 1 cm, and the free-air gradient is about 3 µGal/cm. Estimates assume a fully empty crypt. Partial infill with rubble or soil, a smaller void, or higher-density brick vaulting would reduce the anomaly. The crypt size, host density and host susceptibility are all assumed.

Gravity: the void was modelled as a 5 x 5 m prism from 6 to 9 m depth with a density contrast of about -2.5 g/cc (air in limestone). This gives a peak of about -21 µGal and an anomaly FWHM of about 11 m. The effective noise is about 11.2 µGal, so S/N is about 1.85. That is just below the marginal threshold. Denser limestone (2.6-2.7 g/cc) would give about 22-23 µGal, which is borderline marginal. Repeated readings, careful drift, tide and terrain corrections, and a station spacing of about 2 m could bring it to marginal detectability. A larger or shallower chamber, or adjoining galleries, would raise the signal. Magnetics: limestone is almost non-magnetic (k about 1e-4 SI), so a void produces only hundredths of a nT. This is far below the 2 nT total-field noise and the 0.5 nT gradiometer noise. Magnetic signals at Saqqara would instead come from fired material, debris fill or burnt layers, not from the void itself. Chamber geometry and depth are assumed. GPR or ERT may be better suited to imaging voids at this depth.

Rough forward-model estimates for an assumed air-filled 0.8 x 2 x 0.8 m prism (top 0.5 m, base 1.3 m). Gravity: a density contrast of about -1.9 g/cm3 (clay against air) gives a negative anomaly of about 13 µGal over the centre. Against the 11.2 µGal effective noise (S/N about 1.2) it is not detectable, consistent with earlier microgravity results. Magnetics: the void is a weak susceptibility low, with an assumed clay susceptibility of about 2e-4 SI and air at 0. It gives a total-field anomaly of only about 0.6 nT at 0.5 m sensor height, well below the 2 nT field noise. Gradiometer: the anomaly is about 1.1 nT. Against about 0.51 nT effective noise (S/N about 2), it is only marginal; a dense grid of about 0.25 m (anomaly FWHM about 1.2 m) is needed. Results scale directly with the clay susceptibility, which varies widely. A more magnetic clay or topsoil, or a masonry or brick lining, could make the target clearer, while infilled niches with soil-like fill would reduce the contrast to near zero. Real niche dimensions and depth also matter. GPR or ERT may be better suited to this target.

Gravity peak is in µGal; magnetic and gradient peaks are in nT. The cistern was modelled as an air-filled 9.6 m x 10 m prism from 1 to 4 m depth in clay. Gravity used a density contrast of about -2.0 g/cm3, giving roughly -150 µGal at the centre. With 11.2 µGal noise, S/N is about 13. The anomaly is about 10-12 m wide (FWHM), so use stations every 2 m or less on a grid. Magnetics assumed clay susceptibility of about 2e-4 SI, so the void contrast is tiny. The total-field anomaly of about 1.5 nT is below the 2 nT field noise, and the gradiometer anomaly of about 0.3 nT is below the 0.5 nT noise, so neither method detects it. Results depend on the real clay density and susceptibility, on any water in the cistern (a full cistern halves the gravity contrast), and on the vaulted walls and masonry, which add positive mass and magnetic signal. Cloister walls and buildings also need terrain and building corrections. Nearby iron, pipes and fill will dominate the magnetic data, and a magnetic response could only come from the masonry itself. The total-field anomaly is a dipolar pair at 54.7° inclination.

Gravity was modelled as a 9.6 x 10 m prism from 1 to 4 m depth. I assumed a clay density of about 2.0 g/cc against water at 1.0 g/cc, a contrast of about -1.0 g/cc. This gives roughly -75 µGal over the centre and S/N about 6.7 against 11.2 µGal noise. The anomaly width at half maximum is about 10-12 m, so 2 m stations (1 m over the target if possible) are advised. Wetter or lighter clay (1.7-1.8 g/cc) would cut the anomaly to about 55-60 µGal, which is still detectable. Cistern walls, roof and floor (masonry or concrete) are not modelled; they would modify both the gravity and magnetic responses and could dominate the magnetics. For magnetics I assumed a susceptibility contrast of about -2e-4 SI (water is weakly diamagnetic; clay is typically about 1e-4 to 5e-4 SI). This gives roughly -1.4 nT in total field (S/N under 1) and about -0.3 nT in vertical gradient (S/N about 0.6). Neither is detectable unless the clay is much more magnetic than typical. Gravity results require careful terrain, height (about 3 µGal/cm free-air) and drift corrections. Nearby buildings, basements or slopes could produce comparable signals.

The dyke and the host lavas were both given textbook basalt properties, so there is no density or susceptibility contrast. With no contrast, the forward-modelled anomaly is zero for all three methods, whatever the depth, width or field geometry. S/N is therefore 0 and no station spacing is given. This agrees with the local experience that dykes of normal width are not normally detected by profiling across the Antrim basalts. In reality a weak contrast might exist, for example from differences in magnetite content, weathering of the lavas, remanence of a different polarity or age, or chilled margins. If so, a magnetic gradiometer survey at roughly 0.5 m spacing would be the most sensitive option to try. Detection would still depend on the true contrast being larger than the strong magnetic noise from the near-surface lavas. Gravity would remain hopeless for a 2.5 m wide body with a density contrast of only a few tens of kg/m3.

The pod was modelled as a sphere of 5 m radius with its centre at 20 m depth and a density contrast of +1500 kg/m³. This gives a peak gravity anomaly of about 13 µGal. Effective gravity noise is about 11.2 µGal (5 µGal instrument and 10 µGal field noise in quadrature), so S/N is about 1.2, below the detection threshold. The stated CG-5 has similar precision to the CG-6, so this does not change. The anomaly FWHM would be about 31 m, implying roughly 6 m station spacing if the target were detectable. Detection could become marginal with a larger or shallower pod, or with repeated readings and very careful terrain, drift and tide corrections. Even so, an elongate pod or a pod with lower chromite grade would weaken the anomaly. With no susceptibility contrast specified (peridotite in peridotite), the magnetic and gradiometer anomalies are zero. In practice, serpentinisation-related magnetite in the host can make the pod a magnetic low, but that is not modelled here.

These are rough 2D forward estimates for a vertical, tabular dyke 5 m wide, with its top 1 m deep and extending to 200 m depth. The profile is assumed to run roughly N–S across an E–W strike. Assumed properties: density contrast of about 0.5 g/cc (basalt about 2.85, sandstone about 2.35, reduced for weathering) and susceptibility contrast of about 0.02 SI for weathered basalt against near-zero sandstone. Effective noise is about 11.2 µGal for gravity, about 2 nT for total field and about 0.51 nT for the gradiometer. This gives S/N of about 14 for gravity, about 145 for total field and about 160 for the gradient. The FWHM is about 35 m for gravity and about 5–7 m for total field. Basalt susceptibility varies widely (0.001–0.1 SI) and weathering can strongly reduce magnetite content, so magnetic amplitudes may be several times smaller or larger. They would still be detectable unless the susceptibility falls below about 0.001 SI. Remanent magnetisation, which is common in basalts, could change both the amplitude and the shape of the anomaly, possibly reversing it. If the strike is oblique to magnetic north, the anomaly becomes more dipolar and smaller. Gravity requires terrain and elevation corrections, and its amplitude depends on the assumed depth extent and the degree of weathering. The gradiometer is recommended because it gives the sharpest resolution of the dyke edges and depth, and it suppresses diurnal and regional effects. Total-field magnetics would also work well.

Values come from forward modelling a vertical rectangular prism 60 x 100 m in plan, extending from 30 to 150 m depth, with +1500 kg/m3 density contrast and an apparent susceptibility contrast of 1 SI. Magnetisation is induced only (F = 48563 nT, I = 58.1 deg). Gravity: the peak is about 1.0 mGal (1000 µGal) against 11.2 µGal noise, so S/N is about 90. Total field: the peak is several thousand nT, about 8500 nT. At this inclination it is offset slightly south of the body and paired with a low on the north side. Noise is 2 nT, so S/N is in the thousands. Gradiometer: the peak is about 270 nT against 0.51 nT noise, so S/N is about 500. All three methods detect the target easily. Total-field magnetics is recommended because it is fastest, has the best depth sensitivity and is most diagnostic for magnetite. The gradiometer, with its 1 m baseline and sensor near the ground, has a narrower response that is dominated by shallow sources. Gravity is a useful second method to confirm the ore is a dense mass. Main limitations: (1) At 1 SI, self-demagnetisation is significant and is not modelled. The true anomaly may be roughly 30-50% lower, depending on shape. (2) Remanence in the magnetite could change both the amplitude and the shape of the anomaly. (3) The serpentinite host is itself magnetic and variably serpentinised. This produces strong, short-wavelength geological noise far above instrument noise, which will be the real limit on resolving body edges. (4) Very large gradients over the body may approach the instrument's measuring range. (5) Gravity readings need terrain and Bouguer corrections in the Divriği topography. Station spacings are set for at least 5 stations across each method's half-maximum width: about 120 m for gravity, about 90 m for total field and about 60 m for gradient.

The fault was modelled as a 2D vertical step: a semi-infinite clay-filled block 20–40 m deep (20 m throw) against limestone. Textbook densities were used (clay about 2.2 g/cm³, limestone about 2.55 g/cm³, contrast about -0.35 g/cm³). This gives a full gravity step of 2πGΔρt ≈ 290 µGal. The effective gravity noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 26. The step is spread over roughly 50–60 m, so a station spacing of 10 m or less is recommended. The step will be reduced if the fault dips, the real density contrast is smaller, or the alluvium thickness varies. Careful terrain, drift and tidal corrections are needed, and a precise elevation survey is required (3 cm of height error ≈ 10 µGal). The susceptibility contrast between clay and limestone is tiny (about 1e-4 SI). Over 20–40 m depth this gives a total-field anomaly of only about 1–3 nT, which is below the 2 nT field noise. The vertical gradient over a 1 m baseline is about 0.1 nT, against 0.5 nT noise. Neither magnetic method is useful unless magnetic gravels or remanent units are present. The magnetic amplitudes also depend on the fault strike relative to magnetic north (inclination 57.8°).

Model: 2D vertical contact (step), with clay (about 2.2 g/cc, susceptibility about 2e-4 SI) against marble (about 2.75 g/cc, nearly non-magnetic). Offset unit spans 50 to 600 m depth, so thickness is 550 m and density contrast is about -0.54 g/cc. Gravity: the full step 2*pi*G*drho*t is about 12 mGal against about 11 uGal of noise, so S/N is far above 5. FWHM of the horizontal gradient is about 350 m, so 50 m spacing gives well over 5 stations across it; 50-70 m would suffice, and denser spacing helps locate the fault trace. Magnetics: kF is only about 9 nT, and with a 50 m source depth the contact anomaly is about 2-4 nT, giving S/N of about 1.5-2. That is at best borderline, and the result depends strongly on the clay susceptibility and the fault strike relative to magnetic north. Gradiometer: the vertical gradient over a 1 m baseline from a 50 m deep contact is a few hundredths of a nT, well below 0.5 nT noise. Depths and properties are assumed. Real basin fill is often sandier and more porous, and porosity and saturation will change the density contrast, though gravity remains robust. Terrain corrections at the basin edge and the regional field must be handled in practice.

Gravity was not assessed because the tables give no density for peridotite; the zero values are placeholders, not a finding that gravity would fail. As a rough check, a +0.5 g/cc contrast (peridotite 3.15 vs granite 2.64) would give about 1.6 mGal, which would be clearly detectable. Real kimberlite is often weathered and can be less dense than granite near surface. Magnetic estimates are hand approximations, not a full numerical model. The pipe was treated as a vertical cylinder (radius 100 m, top 20 m, base 600 m). Assumed susceptibility contrast is about 0.15 SI (peridotite ~0.15, granite ~0.0025), with induced magnetisation only and demagnetisation ignored (~5-10% reduction). Because the inclination is low and negative (-29 deg), the total-field response is an asymmetric low/high pair. The low sits roughly over the pipe and the high is offset to the north, so the peak value carries about a factor-of-two uncertainty. The anomaly is about 200 m wide, so 25 m spacing on lines across the pipe in both directions is ample. Gradiometer signals (~10-30 nT) are strongest over the pipe margins, where the anomaly half-width is about 40-60 m; 10 m spacing suits edge mapping. Real kimberlite susceptibility is highly variable and serpentinisation, weathering or remanence could greatly change the amplitude or reverse the sign. Even so, with noise of 2 nT (total field) and 0.5 nT (gradient), detection is robust.

Model: vertical cylinder, radius 750 m, top at 300 m, base at 3000 m. Properties: rock salt density about 2.20 g/cm3 against sandstone about 2.35 g/cm3, a contrast of -0.15 g/cm3. Susceptibilities: salt about -1e-5 SI against sandstone about 4e-4 SI, a contrast of about -4e-4 SI. Gravity: the on-axis gravity low is about -2.6 mGal (2600 µGal) against about 11 µGal noise, so S/N is roughly 230. The anomaly FWHM is about 1.5 to 2 km. Total-field magnetics: the low is only about 5 nT against 2 nT noise, so S/N is about 2.5 (marginal). This result depends strongly on the sandstone susceptibility, which can vary by an order of magnitude, and on any magnetic minerals in the clastics or in evaporite caprock or inclusions. Gradiometer: the 1 m vertical gradient from a source 300 m deep is about 0.01 nT, far below 0.5 nT noise. Gradiometers are unsuitable for deep targets. Gravity caveats: in practice the Sivas Basin density contrasts are complicated. Gypsum or anhydrite caprock and inclusions (up to about 2.9 g/cm3) can reduce or reverse the salt low. Surrounding minibasin fill compaction, regional trends and terrain also matter, so terrain corrections and regional–residual separation are needed. Real diapir shapes (overhangs, stems, welds) will alter the amplitude and width. Station spacing could be relaxed to about 300 to 400 m, with denser coverage over the flanks.

The dyke was modelled as a 2D vertical prism, top 2 m, 3 m wide, base at 202 m, on a profile at right angles to an assumed E-W strike (effective inclination about 69°). Gravity assumes basalt about 2.95 and limestone about 2.55 g/cc (contrast about 0.4). That gives about 73 µGal against 11 µGal noise (S/N about 6.5), with a broad FWHM of about 40 m. Real chalk is lighter (about 2.0-2.3 g/cc), which would increase the contrast. Magnetics assume an average-basalt susceptibility contrast of about 0.07 SI, with chalk near zero, induced magnetisation only. Total field gives about 6600 nT peak, slightly offset from the dyke with a negative flank, and an FWHM of about 6 m. The gradiometer gives about 2100 nT, with an FWHM of about 3-4 m. Basalt susceptibility varies by more than an order of magnitude. Self-demagnetisation is ignored. Antrim basalts can carry strong remanence, which could change the anomaly shape and amplitude greatly; even so, detection is near-certain for any realistic value. The gradiometer response would exceed the Grad601 measurement range (about ±100 nT, or ±1000 nT on the coarse range), so the instrument would saturate over the dyke. For that reason a total-field survey (Overhauser at 0.5 m) is recommended, with lines run at right angles to strike. A gravity survey is feasible but slower and less diagnostic. Weathered dyke tops, other dykes and glacial till with basalt boulders may add noise.

Gravity was modelled as a 2.5D prism 300 m wide, 1000 m long, from 2 to 20 m depth, with a -300 kg/m³ contrast. That gives about -210 µGal over the valley centre (an infinite slab would give about 226 µGal). Effective noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 19, and the anomaly is roughly 300 m wide at half maximum. Real valley fills are often less dense than assumed, or the contrast with weathered shale may be weaker, but even a -100 kg/m³ contrast would stay detectable. Use 50 m station spacing or less, read stations through the valley and well beyond it to fix the background, and apply terrain and elevation corrections with an elevation accuracy of a few cm. The magnetic results assume an assumed susceptibility contrast of about -3e-4 SI between clay and shale. A broad, nearly flat-lying body gives only weak edge effects of about 2 nT in total field and below 0.5 nT in vertical gradient, which is at or below field noise. If the fill contains magnetic gravels or the shale is more magnetic, edge anomalies could be larger, but magnetics is not a reliable method here. Seismic refraction, ERT or TEM would complement gravity for mapping the valley's depth and geometry.

Forward model: the drum is treated as a sphere of equal volume (radius 0.35 m, centre about 1.05 m deep, volume about 0.18 m3), using standard sphere and induced-dipole formulas. Gravity: an air-filled void in soil (density contrast about -1.9 g/cc) gives a deficit of only about 2 µGal. The effective noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 0.2 and gravity cannot see it. Total-field magnetics: with apparent susceptibility 3, F = 46904 nT and inclination 58.3°, the dipole term is about 2000 nT·m3. With the sensor about 1.55 m above the centre, this gives a peak of about 850 nT. The positive peak is offset slightly toward magnetic south, with a negative lobe to the north. The anomaly width at half maximum is about 1.5 m, so S/N is in the hundreds. Gradiometer: about 1600 nT at the lower sensor (1.25 m above the centre) minus about 280 nT at the upper sensor gives roughly 1350 nT. S/N is in the thousands and the anomaly is narrower (half-maximum width about 1 m), so it localises the drum best. However, the anomaly may exceed or approach the Grad601 range on its sensitive setting, so use the ±1000 nT range. The gradiometer also suppresses diurnal and regional variations. Real drums depart from a sphere: shape anisotropy, remanence, corrosion and the effects of several neighbouring drums can change amplitude and shape by a factor of 2 or more. Nearby steel drums at the test site may produce overlapping anomalies. The peak values here are approximate, ±30% or so. Lines should run along the magnetic meridian at about 0.25-0.5 m line spacing.

The valley was modelled as a 60 m wide, 300 m long prism extending from 1 to 15 m depth with a -300 kg/m3 density contrast. Gravity gives a low of about -140 uGal (2D estimate about -147 uGal, slightly reduced by the finite 300 m length) with a FWHM of roughly 60-70 m. Effective gravity noise is about 11 uGal, so S/N is about 12. The magnetic susceptibility contrast between clay and limestone is tiny and uncertain; textbook means are about 1.7e-4 and 3e-4 SI, a contrast of about -1.3e-4 SI. With F = 53263 nT this gives a total-field anomaly of about 2 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 1), and edge gradients of about 0.6 nT against 0.5 nT noise (S/N about 1.2). Magnetic contrast could be larger if the fill contains glacial till with magnetic clasts or the bedrock is more magnetic, but that cannot be relied on. Gravity data need careful elevation (about 3 cm for 10 uGal) and terrain corrections. Lateral density variations in the overburden or a variable bedrock surface can mimic or mask part of the signal. Run lines perpendicular to the valley axis at 10 m spacing (5 m near the margins helps define the walls).

Gravity was modelled as a 2D prism 1000 m wide, from 5 m to 60 m depth, with a -100 kg/m3 contrast. The 5000 m length makes it close to 2D. This gives a broad low of about -220 µGal with a full width at half maximum near 1000 m. Against about 11 µGal noise, that is an S/N of roughly 20. Gravity units are µGal; magnetic and gradient values are in nT. The magnetic values assume a susceptibility contrast of about -4e-4 SI (clay is less magnetic than shale), but textbook values for both overlap widely. Glacial till often carries detrital magnetite, which could reverse or enlarge the contrast, so the magnetic verdicts are highly uncertain. A broad, nearly flat-topped body produces magnetic anomalies only over its edges, not its centre. These edge anomalies are about 8 nT in total field and about 1 nT in the gradiometer reading. They are narrow, so the station spacings are set by the edge anomaly widths rather than by the valley width. Near-surface till boulders and cultural noise will likely mask them. The real valley has sloping sides rather than vertical walls, so its edge anomalies will be broader and weaker than modelled. The fill density contrast is also uncertain: dense till may give a much smaller contrast than assumed, so the gravity anomaly would scale down proportionally. Gravity data need terrain and drift corrections, plus removal of any regional field.

The drum was modelled as a sphere of radius 0.35 m with its centre at 3.35 m depth (volume about 0.18 m3), carrying induced magnetisation only. Gravity: an air-filled void against soil (density contrast about -1.8 g/cc) gives a peak of about -0.19 uGal against 11 uGal noise, so it is not detectable. Magnetics: the given apparent susceptibility of 3 SI, used in the low-susceptibility (k*V*F/mu0) approximation, gives a dipole moment of about 2.2e4 A m2. That yields a peak of about 69,000 nT total field and about 46,000 nT gradient, both with S/N far above 5. These values are physically unrealistic: the total-field figure exceeds the 51,843 nT main field. Real single drums at 3 m typically produce tens to a few hundred nT. The 3 SI 'apparent' value likely already includes demagnetisation and shape effects, or is overstated. Even so, a realistic anomaly of tens of nT would still be clearly detectable with either magnetic method at this depth, consistent with the reported 6-11 ft detection limit. For the total-field survey, the anomaly peaks slightly south of the drum at inclination 67 degrees, with a full width at half maximum of about 3.9 m (about 4 m), hence 0.75 m spacing. The gradiometer anomaly is narrower, about 2.9 m, hence 0.5 m spacing. Expected interference: wall-thickness and corrosion variation and remanence in the drum; nearby buried ferrous debris, fences and utilities; and loss of the gradiometer signal if the drum is deeper than about 3-4 m.

Tank modelled as a sphere of equal volume (10 m³, radius about 1.34 m, centre about 2.34 m deep). Gravity: an air-filled void in soil with a density contrast of about -1.9 g/cm³ gives a peak of about -23 µGal. Against about 11 µGal of noise that is S/N ≈ 2, so marginal. The steel shell would partly offset this, and a fluid-filled tank would give almost no signal. Magnetics: induced dipole with an apparent susceptibility of 3 in a 51843 nT field at 67° inclination. The point-dipole formula gives a total-field peak of about 9,600 nT and a gradiometer difference of about 8,500 nT. Both are far above noise. These values are overestimates because the sensor is so close to a body of this size; the real tank's apparent susceptibility, remanence and demagnetisation effects matter more. A fluxgate gradiometer will likely saturate over the tank, so this gives an upper bound. The anomaly is dipolar, with the positive peak offset slightly south and a negative lobe to the north. Nearby fences, pipes, vehicles and buried scrap metal will give similar anomalies, so ground truthing with GPR or EM is advised.

Model: horizontal cylinder of radius 0.3 m with its axis at 1.8 m depth, assumed to strike E-W and be crossed by a N-S profile. Gravity: air-filled void in soil (density contrast about -1.9 g/cc) gives a peak of about -4 µGal against about 11 µGal noise (S/N about 0.4), so not detectable; the steel wall would partly cancel this deficit anyway. Total field: induced only, apparent susceptibility 2 in the transverse limit, F = 49701 nT, inclination 68.3°. The 2D line-dipole peak is about 770 nT at a sensor height of 0.5 m against 2 nT noise (S/N about 380). Gradiometer: lower minus upper sensor (2.0 m and 3.0 m above the axis) gives about 570 nT against 0.5 nT noise (S/N over 1000). Anomaly half-widths are about 2-3 m, so station spacings are 0.25-0.5 m with lines about 1 m apart. In practice, joint welds, remanence, cathodic protection and buried ferrous debris will add strong, variable responses. A pipe striking N-S would give a weaker anomaly with a different shape. Fluxgate gradiometers may saturate over very large anomalies. Cover depth and diameter are assumed.

Target modelled as a sphere of radius 0.08 m, centre 0.48 m deep. For gravity, an air-filled void in soil was taken as a density contrast of about -1.9 g/cc. That gives a mass deficit of about 4 kg and a peak of about 0.1 µGal, far below the roughly 11 µGal noise. For magnetics, the stated apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI was used directly as an induced dipole. Demagnetisation is assumed to be already included in the apparent value. That gives a moment of about 0.23 A·m² in a 45088 nT field at 55° inclination. The peak factor relative to the polar value was estimated rather than computed (about 1.6). The total-field peak is about 40 nT at 0.5 m sensor height, S/N about 20. The gradiometer peak is about 110 nT at 0.2 m lower-sensor height with a 1 m baseline, S/N about 200. The anomaly is offset slightly south of the target, with a weak negative lobe to the north. Real shells may carry remanence and shape anisotropy, which can change amplitude and polarity by a factor of 2 or more. The gradiometer anomaly half-width is only about 0.6 m. Line spacing should be about 0.25-0.5 m with dense along-line sampling (≤0.1 m). Nearby ferrous debris or magnetic soils could produce false positives.

Estimates use the stated model: the bomb is treated as a sphere of equal volume (radius 0.34 m, about 0.165 m³) centred about 1.84 m below ground, with an apparent susceptibility of 3 SI and induced magnetisation only. The 51,890 nT field at 71.7° inclination was used. The magnetic sensors are 2 m above ground, so the source distance is about 3.84 m for the lower sensor and 4.84 m for the upper one. The total-field peak is about 67 nT, which gives S/N of about 33 against 2 nT noise. The anomaly width at half maximum is about 3.8 m. The positive peak sits slightly south of the bomb, with a weaker negative lobe to the north. The gradiometer reading (lower minus upper sensor) is about 33 nT against about 0.5 nT noise, so S/N is about 65. It also gives a narrower anomaly and suppresses regional and diurnal variation, so it is preferred. Gravity was modelled with the stated air-in-soil contrast of about -1.9 g/cm³. A real steel and explosive bomb would have a positive contrast of a similar size, so the result would be similar. Either way the anomaly is under 1 µGal, far below the 11 µGal noise. Real UXO often carries remanent magnetisation and is elongated, which can change the amplitude by a factor of 2 or more and distort the anomaly shape. Ferrous battlefield debris will produce many similar anomalies. In practice, keep line spacing at or below about 0.75 m and hold drone altitude steady, since the signal falls off roughly with the cube of distance. The site is a WWII front line, so any intrusive checks must follow EOD safety procedures.

The target was modelled as a sphere of radius 0.34 m with its centre about 4.04 m below the seabed, giving a volume of about 0.165 m³. Gravity: taking the stated air fill against sand (about -2.0 g/cc), the anomaly at the seabed is about -0.13 µGal against 11 µGal noise, so it cannot be detected. A real steel bomb would be just as undetectable by gravity. Total field: induced dipole with apparent susceptibility 3 SI, moment about 2×10⁴ A·m². At 8.04 m from the centre, the peak at 68.8° inclination is about 6.8 nT, offset slightly south of the target. Against about 2 nT noise, S/N is about 3.4 (marginal). FWHM is about 8 m, so stations about 1.6 m apart. Gradiometer (sensors at 4 m and 5 m above seabed): about 6.8 − 4.8 ≈ 2.0 nT against 0.51 nT noise, S/N about 4 (marginal). FWHM is about 6–7 m, so stations about 1.3 m apart. Real-world factors not modelled: an elongated steel casing, demagnetisation and remanence could change the amplitude by a factor of 2 or more. A deeper burial (4 m rather than 2 m) or the vessel or ROV's own magnetic signature would reduce S/N. Sensor altitude matters most: the anomaly falls off roughly as distance cubed, so flying lower would greatly improve detection. Line spacing should match the along-line station spacing. A Grad601 is not a marine instrument, so a real survey would use marine magnetometer or gradiometer arrays.

Modelled as a sphere of equal volume (radius 0.08 m, centre 0.48 m deep, V ≈ 0.0021 m³). Gravity: the stated target material is air, so I used a density contrast of about -1.9 g/cm³ against soil; a real steel shell would give a positive contrast, but either way the anomaly is only about 0.1 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise. Magnetics: induced dipole with apparent susceptibility 3 in a 45088 nT field at inclination 55°, giving a moment of about 0.23 A·m². With the sensor 2 m up, the source is 2.48 m away. The total-field peak is about 2.3 nT on the south side, against 2.0 nT noise (S/N about 1.1), so it is not detectable. Gradiometer: lower sensor at 2.48 m and upper at 3.48 m give a difference of about 1.5 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 2.9), so it is marginal. Its anomaly half-width is about 2.5 m, so 0.5 m line and station spacing is suggested. Fluxgate gradiometer readings from a 2 m drone carry extra noise from platform motion, orientation and heading errors, which could make detection worse. Remanence in real ordnance could raise or lower the anomaly. Flying lower, ideally under 1 m, would improve detectability greatly, because the anomaly falls off with the cube of distance or faster.

The target was modelled as a 0.4 m equal-volume sphere centred at 3.2 m depth, with induced magnetisation only (apparent susceptibility 3 SI, F = 49490 nT, I = 66.7°). Gravity used the stated air-in-soil contrast of about -1.9 g/cc and gives about -0.04 µGal, far below the 11 µGal noise. Even a solid steel contrast would only reach about 0.1 µGal. Total field: peak about +13.8 nT, displaced about 0.7 m south of the target, against 2 nT noise (S/N about 7). Gradiometer: about 9.6 nT against 0.5 nT noise (S/N about 19), so it is the more robust choice, but the anomaly is narrow (FWHM about 2.5-3 m), so lines must also be closely spaced (≤0.5-1 m). Remanent magnetisation, bomb orientation and an elongated shape can change both the amplitude (by roughly ±2×) and the anomaly shape. Nearby surface scrap iron, cultural noise and magnetic soils can mask the signal. At depths much beyond 3-4 m the anomaly falls off as 1/r³ and detection degrades quickly. Borehole magnetometry is preferable for deeper clearance.

I modelled the cavity as an air-filled sphere 4 m across, with its top 5 m down (centre at 7 m), in gypsum. Gravity: the cavity is 2350 kg/m³ lighter than the gypsum around it. That gives a low of about -10.7 µGal. The effective noise is about 11.2 µGal (5 µGal per reading and 10 µGal field noise combined), so S/N is about 0.96. That is below the threshold of 2, so it is not detectable. Magnetics: gypsum is almost non-magnetic (susceptibility contrast about 1e-5 SI). The total-field anomaly is about 0.005 nT against 2 nT of noise, and the gradient anomaly is about 0.002 nT against 0.51 nT. Neither is detectable, so no magnetic method is worth using. All station spacings are 0 because nothing is detectable; if you still ran a trial gravity grid, the model suggests about 2 m spacing. I used approximate Sivas coordinates (39.75 N, 37.02 E) and the tool's own model of the Earth's magnetic field, not your exact 48567 nT / 58.4° figures. The difference doesn't matter because the magnetic signal is negligible either way. The 4 m size is an assumed scale for the dissolution spaces, not a measured value. A cavity that is shallower, larger or elongated, or a group of several, would give a stronger gravity signal. One of about 5 m diameter or more at this depth, or a 4 m cavity nearer the surface, would probably be marginal or better. On the other hand, real gravity surveys need terrain and building corrections, which could add extra noise on a building plot.
