The tool took the main field from the site location and date rather than the 49112 nT / 66.5° values given, but that has almost no effect on such a small magnetic signal. Real gravity work would need terrain, building and traffic corrections, and urban noise in London may be higher than the standard 10 µGal assumed here.

Modelled as an air-filled horizontal cylinder crossing the profile at right angles, 1.5 m in diameter with its top at 8 m depth in gravel, under the standard instrument conditions. The size and depth are assumptions. Gravity: the density contrast of -2000 kg/m³ gives a peak of about -5.4 µGal. The noise is 11.2 µGal (5 µGal per reading plus 10 µGal field noise), so S/N is about 0.48: not detectable. Magnetics: the material tables have no susceptibility for gravel, so I assumed a contrast of -0.001 SI (air replacing slightly magnetic gravel). That gives about -0.12 nT for total field (S/N about 0.06) and about -0.027 nT for the gradiometer (S/N about 0.05). Neither is detectable. The magnetic result scales directly with the susceptibility contrast, so the gradiometer would need a contrast about 100 times larger before it became even marginal. That could happen if the gravel is rich in volcanic clasts, but it is unlikely. The main field was calculated from the Tehran coordinates and a 2025 date in the field model, not from the 48858 nT, 54.8° inclination and 5.0° declination you gave. These values should be similar, and the difference is very unlikely to change the verdicts. A spacing of 0 means not detectable. If the tunnel is detectable, the modelled anomaly width implies about 2 m station spacing. A tunnel this small and this deep is beyond reach. For an air-filled 1.5 m cylinder, gravity becomes marginal only at about 4 m to the top and clearly detectable only at about 2 m, under these noise levels. Better targets are features nearer the surface: collapsed sections, the qanat's vertical access shafts (which may also show a magnetic response from debris or lining), or larger chambers. GPR or electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) are worth considering. Microgravity would only help with a tunnel no deeper than about 2 to 4 m, or with much lower noise from repeated readings and careful terrain and drift correction.

I modelled the chamber as an air-filled 6 x 6 x 6 m block with its top 6 m and base 12 m below the station, inside homogeneous soil. The density contrast is -1920 kg/m³. Gravity: the peak is about -34 µGal against about 11.2 µGal of noise, so S/N is about 3.0. That makes it marginal, not clearly detectable. Use 2 m stations or closer, take repeat readings and correct carefully for terrain. On a steep-sided mound the terrain and mound-shape corrections will be large compared with a 34 µGal signal. The magnetic results depend on a value I assumed. The tool has no table susceptibility for soil, so I set the air-minus-soil contrast to -0.001 SI. On that assumption the total-field peak is about -1.7 nT (S/N about 0.9) and the gradiometer peak is about -0.49 nT (S/N about 1.0). Neither method would detect the chamber, so no station spacing is given; the tool's 1 m figure would only matter if the anomaly could be seen. If the real mound fill is more magnetic, or more mixed, than assumed, the magnetic numbers change in proportion, but stone and turf layers would probably add near-surface clutter that hides a deep void. I used the tool's own main field for the site with a mid-2024 date, not the 49570 nT / 68° / -1.4° you gave. These should be close, but I did not check the difference. Microgravity, possibly combined with ERT or GPR, is the only one of these methods with a realistic chance of finding the chamber.

I modelled the crypt as an air-filled rectangular block in clay. It is 4 m wide along the profile and 6 m across it, with its top at 1 m and its base at 3.5 m. The model used standard instrument noise and induced magnetisation only. Gravity: the model gives a mass deficit of about -88 µGal against 11.2 µGal of noise (S/N about 7.9), so the crypt should be clearly detectable. Take readings about 1 m apart on a grid. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 1.5 nT against 2 nT of noise (S/N about 0.76), so it is not detectable. Gradiometer: the peak is about 0.81 nT against 0.51 nT of noise (S/N about 1.6), so it is also not detectable. The air-to-clay susceptibility contrast is only about -0.0002 SI. Things to keep in mind: (1) I entered approximate coordinates for Pukanec and a 2024 date, not the field values you gave (49407 nT, inclination 65.1°). The field the tool used should be similar, but this was not checked, and it hardly matters for the magnetic results because the contrast is so small. (2) The tool assumed a clay density of about 2210 kg/m³, so the -2210 kg/m³ contrast treats the crypt as completely empty. Crypt and cellar walls, vaults, rubble or a partial fill would shrink the anomaly. Since the crypt size and host were both assumptions, the true anomaly could be well below 88 µGal. (3) Inside a church you need terrain corrections for the walls, pillars and building mass, steps and floor levels, careful drift and tide control, and repeat readings. Steel, heating pipes and wiring would also swamp any magnetic signal. (4) GPR is often a useful companion to gravity for finding shallow crypts under floors.

None of the three methods would reliably detect these niches with standard field equipment. I modelled each niche as an air-filled block in clay: 0.8 m wide along the profile, 2 m long across it, top at 0.5 m and bottom at 1.3 m. The niche size is an assumption. The model used a density contrast of -2210 kg/m³ and a susceptibility contrast of -0.0002 SI. Gravity: the peak is a low of about -15.7 µGal against about 11.2 µGal of noise, so S/N is about 1.4 and the target is not detectable. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 0.44 nT against 2 nT of noise, so S/N is about 0.2 and it is not detectable. Magnetic gradient: the peak is about 0.61 nT against 0.51 nT of noise, so S/N is about 1.2 and it is not detectable. The station spacing is given as 0 because no method detects the target. If a survey were attempted anyway, the anomalies are so narrow that stations would need to be about 0.2 m apart. The model looked up the main magnetic field from the site's coordinates and an assumed 2024 date rather than taking the 49407 nT, 65.1° inclination you gave. The two should be very similar, and the magnetic signal is limited by clay's weak susceptibility anyway. The results assume induced magnetisation only. Several niches side by side, larger voids, wall linings, iron coffin fittings or a stronger susceptibility contrast in the clay could make the target easier to see. Close-spaced magnetic gradiometry might then pick up the fittings. Ground-penetrating radar is usually better suited to voids this shallow and this small, though it was not part of this assessment. These results agree with the earlier finding that microgravity cannot reliably detect the niches.

I modelled the chamber as an empty 5 m x 5 m block from 6 m to 9 m depth in limestone. Air against limestone gives a density contrast of about -2550 kg/m3 and a susceptibility contrast of about -0.0003 SI. Gravity: the void gives a low of about 21 µGal. Effective noise is about 11.2 µGal (5 µGal reading and 10 µGal field noise combined), so S/N is about 1.9. That is just below the marginal threshold of 2, so the verdict is not detectable. If the target were detectable, readings 2 m apart would be needed. Careful work could bring field noise down: repeat readings, tight drift loops, precise levelling and a good terrain correction. Then the chamber might become marginal. A larger, shallower or linked set of galleries would also give a stronger signal. The residual low you already have could come from several chambers or galleries together rather than one 5 m room. Magnetics: limestone is almost non-magnetic, so the void gives only about 0.17 nT in total field (S/N about 0.08) and about 0.055 nT in the gradient (S/N about 0.11). Neither is detectable unless the chamber holds magnetic fill or objects. Station spacing is given as 0 for all three because none is detectable. The site location was entered as coordinates of about 29.87 N, 31.21 E. The model then took the main field from a standard global field model rather than the values you gave (43939 nT, inclination 44.7°). Any difference should be small and would not change the magnetic verdicts. The chamber size and depth are assumptions.

I modelled the empty cistern as an air-filled block 9.6 m by 10 m in plan, from 1 m to 4 m deep, in clay. The model used a density contrast of -2210 kg/m³ and a susceptibility contrast of -0.0002 SI. The magnetic field came from a location near Valencia (39.47 N, 0.38 W) on 2024-06-01. Gravity should show a low of about -165 µGal against about 11 µGal of noise (S/N about 15), so it is clearly detectable; stations every 2 m or closer will define the low. Total-field magnetics would give only about 1.7 nT against about 2 nT of noise (S/N about 0.9), and the gradiometer about 0.67 nT against about 0.51 nT (S/N about 1.3), so neither would detect it. That is why their station spacing is given as 0. In practice, gravity readings need terrain and building corrections, because the cloister walls, columns and nearby buildings produce their own gravity effects. These effects could be similar in size to the cistern's signal. A thick vaulted ceiling, a partly filled or water-filled cistern, or a different host density would reduce the anomaly. Iron fittings, drains or other metal under the pavement would produce magnetic anomalies that could hide or be mistaken for the cistern.

I modelled the cistern as a water-filled rectangular block in clay: top at 1 m, bottom at 4 m, 9.6 m across the profile and 10 m along it. I used textbook values, giving a density contrast of about -1210 kg/m3 and a susceptibility contrast of about -0.0002 SI. The tool's absolute peaks were about 90.4 µGal for gravity, 1.71 nT for total field and 0.67 nT for the gradient. I gave them as negative because water is less dense and less magnetic than clay, so the anomalies are lows. Gravity should clearly detect it: the low is about 90 µGal against about 11.2 µGal of combined noise (S/N about 8). Use stations about 2 m apart on lines over the target. Neither magnetic method would detect it. Total field gives about 1.7 nT against 2 nT of noise (S/N about 0.9), and the gradiometer gives about 0.67 nT against about 0.51 nT (S/N about 1.3). I set their station spacing to 0 for that reason. I didn't enter the field values you gave (45096 nT, inclination 54.7°, declination 1.4°). The tool calculated the main field itself from an approximate site location (39.47 N, 0.38 W) and an assumed date of 1 January 2024. That field should be close to yours, and since the magnetic signals are well below the noise, the verdicts wouldn't change. Things that could change the answer: if the cistern is only partly full, or the clay density differs from the textbook value, the gravity low will be smaller. A shallower top would make it bigger. Masonry or steel in the walls, or any remanent magnetisation, could produce magnetic anomalies not included here. Terrain or nearby buildings would need gravity corrections. Using a 2 m spacing in both directions would map the edges of the cistern.

All three methods should detect the dyke clearly. The magnetic gradiometer is recommended: it has the highest signal-to-noise ratio (S/N ≈ 311) and gives the sharpest outline of a 3 m wide dyke whose top is about 2 m down. Total-field magnetics also works very well (S/N ≈ 260). Gravity works too, but with much less margin (S/N ≈ 7). The model is a 2D dyke 3 m wide, running from 2 m to 200 m depth at right angles to the survey line. The density difference used was 440 kg/m³, with chalk taken as limestone. Real chalk is often lighter and more porous, which would make the gravity anomaly larger. The magnetic susceptibility contrast used was 0.07 SI, a typical textbook value, and only induced magnetisation was modelled. Antrim basalts often carry strong remanent magnetisation, which may be reversed, so the size and even the sign of the magnetic anomalies may differ from the model. The Earth's magnetic field was worked out by the tool from an approximate Antrim latitude, longitude and survey date. It was not checked directly against the field you gave (49895 nT, inclination 68.9°, declination -1.4°), but the two should be very close. Results assume flat ground and no regional trend. If the survey line crosses the dyke at an angle, the anomaly gets wider, and a dip in the dyke makes the anomaly lopsided. Glacial till cover or nearby basalt flows could add magnetic noise.

I modelled the target as a vertical dyke 2.5 m wide, with its top at 1 m and its base at 200 m depth. The dyke and the host lavas were both given the same textbook basalt properties, so there is no density or susceptibility difference between them. With no contrast, all three methods give an anomaly of exactly zero: gravity 0 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise, total-field magnetics 0 nT against 2.0 nT noise, and gradiometer 0 nT against 0.51 nT noise. None of the methods would detect it, so no station spacing applies. This fits the field experience that dykes of normal 2-3 m width are not usually found by profiling across the basalts. I did not enter the given main field (49895 nT, inclination 68.9°, declination -1.4°); the tool used a default field for an approximate Antrim location. With zero contrast the field cannot change the result, but the model would need rerunning with the given field if a contrast is introduced. A real dyke could still be detectable if it differs from the lavas in ways the model leaves out. Examples are remanent magnetisation, especially reversed polarity, different magnetite content, chilled or baked margins, or weathering that leaves a soil- or clay-filled trench. If a dyke has to be found, a test line with a fluxgate gradiometer or Overhauser magnetometer at close spacing (about 0.5-1 m) is the cheapest way to check for any real magnetic contrast. Gravity is unlikely to help.

None of the three methods would detect this room with standard field equipment. I modelled it as a 5 m x 5 m air-filled block from 10 m to 13 m depth, using the -1700 kg/m³ density contrast you gave. Gravity: the peak is about -6.2 µGal against about 11.2 µGal effective noise (S/N about 0.56). Station spacing is 0 because the target isn't detectable; if you did survey for it, the model suggests about 2 m. Magnetics: soil has no susceptibility in the tool's tables, so I assumed a typical textbook soil susceptibility of about 0.001 SI, giving a contrast of -0.001 SI. That gives about 0.24 nT for total field (S/N about 0.12) and about 0.056 nT for the gradiometer (S/N about 0.11). Real Cappadocian tuff can be much more magnetic than this. Even so, the contrast would need to be roughly 40-50 times larger before total-field or gradiometer readings reached the 'clearly detectable' level, and the depth makes this unlikely. The magnetic field came from the site latitude, longitude and a 2025 date, which should match the 47895 nT / 56.9° field you quoted. The room size, the 1.7 g/cm³ tuff density and the susceptibility are all assumptions. Gravity would only become marginal (S/N 2 or more) if the room were about 4 times larger in volume or nearer the surface, or if repeat readings cut the noise to about 3 µGal or less. Nearby rooms and tunnels linked to this one could add up to a larger, detectable low. Rough ground also needs a terrain correction. For a single room at 10 m, it's worth looking at ERT or GPR, if the tuff's conductivity allows, or at microgravity with dense repeat readings.

All three methods should clearly detect the dyke. These figures come from one forward model of a vertical dyke 5 m wide, with its top at 1 m and its base at 200 m depth. The model uses textbook contrasts for basalt against sandstone: a density contrast of about 640 kg/m³ and a susceptibility contrast of about 0.070 SI. It assumes induced magnetisation only. The main magnetic field came from the tool's built-in reference field model for Heldburg (about 50.28°N, 10.73°E), using an assumed date of 1 Jan 2024 because the brief gave no date. I did not enter the 49,344 nT, 66.2° inclination and 4.3° declination you gave. The model's field at this site should be close to those values, but this is not confirmed, so the magnetic peaks are approximate. Signal-to-noise ratios: gravity about 206 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise (S/N about 18). Total-field magnetics about 985 nT against 2 nT (S/N about 490). Vertical gradient about 306 nT against 0.51 nT (S/N about 600). I recommend the gradiometer because it gives the sharpest anomaly over a shallow, narrow body. It also suppresses regional and daily field variations, which helps when mapping the dyke's edges, strike and depth. Total-field profiles at 1 m spacing would also work well. Gravity at 5 m spacing would only be useful as an independent check. Weathering of the basalt can reduce both its susceptibility and its density, so real anomalies may be noticeably smaller, although they would still be detectable. Basalt often carries remanent magnetisation, which the model ignores. Remanence can change the anomaly's amplitude, shape and polarity, so the magnetic peaks are uncertain by roughly ±50% or more. The dyke width of 5 m is assumed, and so are the vertical dip and the 200 m depth extent. Magnetic, iron-rich soil or debris near the surface may add short-wavelength noise to the gradiometer data. The 1 m magnetic and gradient spacings meet the rule of at least 5 stations across the anomaly. In practice, gradiometers record continuously along the line, and 0.25–0.5 m sampling along lines a few metres apart works well for mapping the dyke's trend.

Gravity was not modelled. The tables have no density for peridotite, so no gravity anomaly was calculated. The gravity values given here (0, not detectable, 0 m spacing) are placeholders only, not a real verdict. Kimberlite often differs in density from granite, so gravity could still work if a measured density contrast is supplied. Magnetics: the pipe was modelled as a vertical cylinder 200 m across, from 20 m to 600 m depth. The magnetic susceptibility contrast against granite is 0.1475 SI (from typical peridotite values), with induced magnetisation only. Total-field magnetics gives a peak of about 860 nT against 2 nT effective noise (S/N about 430). This is clearly detectable; use stations no more than 50 m apart. The gradiometer gives a peak of about 25 nT against 0.51 nT effective noise (S/N about 49). This is also clearly detectable, with stations no more than 20 m apart. The main field was calculated from an approximate site location (6.5°S, 36.5°W, date 2024-01-01), not from the values you gave (26078 nT, inclination -29.2°). The two should be similar, but the anomaly shape and size may differ slightly. Real kimberlites can be strongly weathered near the surface, which can lower their susceptibility, and they may carry remanent magnetisation. Either could change the amplitude, shape or sign of the anomaly. Peridotite is only a stand-in for kimberlite, and the textbook susceptibility used may overestimate the signal. Even so, the large S/N leaves plenty of margin.

None of the three methods would reliably detect this pod. The pod was modelled as a sphere 10 m across with its top 15 m below the surface and a density contrast of +1500 kg/m³. The modelled gravity peak is about 13.1 µGal. Standard gravity noise is 5 µGal per reading plus 10 µGal of field noise, about 11.2 µGal in total. That gives a signal-to-noise ratio of about 1.2, so gravity is not detectable and the spacing is given as 0. If you surveyed it anyway, the anomaly would be about 10–15 m wide at half its peak, so stations about 5 m apart would be needed. The two magnetic methods were modelled with zero contrast, because the target and host are both peridotite and you said there is no magnetic contrast. With induced magnetisation only, both magnetic anomalies are zero. The modelled main field was taken from the site location (37.07°N, 36.25°E) and a 2025 date; the field values you gave were not entered directly, but this does not affect the zero result. Real chromite pods often sit in serpentinised, magnetite-bearing peridotite, or have magnetite at their edges. That can create a magnetic contrast, often a low, which this model does not include. The noise figures are for a CG-6; a CG-5 has similar or slightly higher reading noise, so the gravity result would not improve. Gravity could become marginal or detectable if the pod is shallower or larger, if field noise is reduced by repeat readings, careful terrain corrections and drift control, or if the pod is long rather than compact.

Modelled as a vertical contact, with the offset clay unit 20–40 m deep against limestone. The tool's textbook properties give a density contrast of about −340 kg/m³ and a susceptibility contrast of about −1e-4 SI. Gravity: a step of about 268 µGal against about 11.2 µGal effective noise (S/N about 24), so it is clearly detectable. Use stations about 10 m apart or closer, and extend the profile well beyond both sides of the fault to define the full step. Total-field magnetics: about 0.49 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 0.25), not detectable. Gradiometer: about 0.017 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 0.03), not detectable. The magnetic results rest on a very small susceptibility contrast. The main magnetic field came from the tool's built-in model for Eskişehir (39.78°N, 30.52°E, 2024), not from the field values you gave. Those values should be very similar, and the magnetic verdicts would not change. Real alluvium over a bedrock valley differs from this model: the depths and 20 m throw are assumed, real densities vary, and alluvium thickness changes and regional trends can hide or mimic the step. You will need terrain and regional corrections.

All three methods would clearly detect this ore body. The target was modelled as a rectangular block with its top at 30 m and its base at 150 m. It is 60 m wide along the profile and 100 m long across it. I used the assumed contrasts of +1500 kg/m³ and 1.0 SI, with induced magnetisation only. Gravity gives about 1.02 mGal, which is a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of about 91. Total-field magnetics gives about 7360 nT (S/N about 3680), and the gradiometer gives about 250 nT (S/N about 490). Total-field magnetics is recommended. Gravity is a strong independent check on the ore's mass and tonnage. I gave the site location (about 39.37°N, 38.12°E, date 2024-06-01) rather than entering the stated main field directly. The 48563 nT, 58.1° inclination and 6.3° declination you gave should be close to the field the tool used, so the results should change very little. With a susceptibility of 1 SI, self-demagnetisation becomes important, and the model does not include it. This means the real anomaly may be smaller and its shape distorted. Divriği magnetite ores may also carry strong remanence, which would change the anomaly's shape, sign and peak; remanence was not modelled. Serpentinite host rock is often magnetic and can produce strong, variable background signals that may partly hide or distort the target's anomaly. Gravity needs terrain corrections in the rugged ground at Divriği. Old workings and open pits could also affect all three methods. Extend the profiles well beyond the 60 m by 100 m footprint so that the full anomaly and its background are recorded.

Gravity is the method to use. The model treats the fault as a vertical contact with clay (sediment) against marble from 50 m to 600 m depth. That gives a density contrast of about -540 kg/m³ and a gravity step of about 11.9 mGal. The estimated noise is about 11 µGal, so S/N is about 1066 and the fault is clearly detectable. Stations every 100 m or closer are enough, with tighter spacing near the fault trace to locate it. In practice, terrain, regional trend and changes in density within the basin fill will matter more than instrument noise. Marble had no susceptibility value in the tool's tables, so I entered an assumed clay-minus-marble contrast of 2e-4 SI. On that assumption the total-field magnetic anomaly is about 3.5 nT, S/N about 1.8, so not detectable. The gradiometer anomaly is about 0.026 nT, S/N about 0.05, so also not detectable. If the susceptibility contrast is really larger, for example from magnetic minerals in the basin fill, total-field magnetics could become marginal. The depths, the vertical fault shape and the textbook properties are all assumptions. The tool set the main magnetic field from the site's latitude and longitude and a 2024 date, not from the values you gave.

I modelled the diapir as a vertical cylinder 1500 m across, with its top at 300 m and its base at 3000 m. It is rock salt inside sandstone, using textbook values: a density contrast of about -130 kg/m³ and a susceptibility contrast of about -0.00041 SI. Only induced magnetisation is included. The main magnetic field came from the tool's model for Sivas (39.75°N, 37.0°E, with an assumed date of 2024). I did not enter the 48567 nT, 58.4° inclination and 6.3° declination you gave, so the magnetic peaks may differ slightly from yours. Gravity: the salt gives a low of about -2.26 mGal. Against 11.2 µGal of effective noise, that is a signal-to-noise ratio of about 200, so it is clearly detectable. A 200 m station spacing is enough, and a closer spacing helps over the edges of the diapir. Real gravity anomalies over salt can be smaller or more complicated than this model. That can happen where there is a dense caprock of gypsum or anhydrite, where the sandstone becomes denser with depth, where there are nearby minibasins, or where there is a regional trend. You will need terrain corrections and a regional–residual separation. Total-field magnetics: the salt gives a low of about 5.3 nT. Against 2 nT of noise, that is a signal-to-noise ratio of about 2.6, so it is only marginal. Any magnetic variation within the host rocks, or volcanic or ophiolitic material in the basin, would probably hide it. Magnetic gradiometer: the signal is about 0.012 nT, far below the 0.5 nT noise, so it is not detectable. A short-baseline gradiometer cannot pick up a body this broad and deep. The answer is a ground or airborne gravity survey, which could be backed up with seismic or MT data to fix the diapir's shape.

I modelled the valley as a 60 m wide (along the profile) by 300 m long rectangular block of clay in limestone, running from 1 m to 15 m depth, with a density contrast of -300 kg/m³. Gravity: the valley gives a low of about 147 µGal against about 11.2 µGal of noise (S/N about 13), so it is clearly detectable. A station spacing of 10 m or less across the valley axis will resolve it. Total-field magnetics and the gradiometer: the susceptibility contrast between clay and limestone is tiny (about -1e-4 SI, from textbook values). The peaks are only about 1.7 nT (S/N about 0.84) and about 0.38 nT (S/N about 0.74), so neither method can see the valley, and I gave 0 m spacing for both. The magnetic run used the IGRF field for Ottawa (45.42°N, 75.70°W) on 1 Jan 2025, not the field values you gave, but the difference should be small. Other cautions: the 60 m width is an assumption, and a narrower valley or more gradual side slopes would give a smaller, broader gravity anomaly. Real overburden and limestone densities vary from place to place. You will also need careful elevation, terrain and drift corrections, and should remove any regional trend. Magnetic clasts in glacial till could add noise, and drilling or seismic work should be used to confirm the bedrock depth.

I modelled the valley as a rectangular block: 300 m wide along the profile, 1000 m long across it, from 2 m to 20 m deep. The density contrast is -300 kg/m³, and the clay-in-shale magnetic susceptibility contrast comes from textbook tables (about -0.0004 SI). The tool took the main field from the site position (lat 38.5, lon -98) and date (2024). I did not check its values against the 51358 nT, 66.3° inclination and 1.7° declination you gave, but small differences should not change the verdicts. Gravity gives a low of about -215 µGal against 11.2 µGal noise (S/N about 19), so it should show up clearly. Total-field magnetics gives about 5.9 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 2.9), which is only marginal. The gradiometer gives about 0.8 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 1.6), which is too weak to detect. All three verdicts assume induced magnetisation only, no remanence, flat ground, a uniform host and no regional trend. A real valley has sloping sides and an irregular base, so the true anomaly will look different. In Kansas, regional gravity and magnetic trends from deeper rocks could hide or distort a broad 300 m feature. You will need regional removal, terrain corrections and a profile well beyond both valley edges, with a few hundred metres of background on each side. The 50 m spacing is the coarsest that resolves the main low. Closer stations near the edges would help map the valley walls. The 300 m width is your assumption, and a narrower valley would give a smaller, sharper anomaly.

Modelled with the check_detectability tool. The drum was treated as a sphere 0.7 m across with its top at 0.7 m. It was given an apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI (the permeable-sphere limit), with induced magnetisation only. Results: gravity about -2.1 µGal against about 11.2 µGal noise (S/N about 0.19), so not detectable. Total field about 858 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 430). Gradiometer about 1370 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 2690). The gradiometer is recommended: it gives the sharpest, most local anomaly and cancels the main field and regional variations. Station or line spacing should be about 0.2 m. I gave the tool an assumed location (42.5°N, 12.5°E, 1 Jan 2020) rather than your field values (46904 nT, inclination 58.3°, declination 4.0°). The output doesn't show which main field was used, so the magnetic numbers may differ slightly from a model run on your values. Treating the drum as air-filled (density contrast -1920 kg/m³) makes the gravity estimate rough, but a few µGal would be undetectable either way. Real drums carry remanence and have a shape effect, which can change the amplitude and the anomaly pattern by a large factor. Corrosion lowers the response. Other buried metal on the site may also overlap with the drum anomaly. With an S/N this high, though, magnetic detection is reliable.

I modelled the drum as a sphere 0.7 m across with its top 3 m down, sitting in soil. I used an apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI (induced magnetisation only) and an air-filled interior, which gives a density contrast of about -1920 kg/m³. The tool did not take the field values you supplied. It worked out the main field from an assumed central Illinois location (40°N, 89°W) and the date 2024-01-01. That should be close to the 51843 nT, 67° inclination field you gave, but it was not checked. Gravity: the peak is about 0.2 µGal against about 11 µGal of noise (S/N about 0.02), so it is not detectable. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 69 nT against about 2 nT of noise (S/N about 35), so it is clearly detectable. Gradiometer: the peak is about 47 nT against about 0.5 nT of noise (S/N about 92), so it is also clearly detectable. The gradiometer has the best S/N and is the least affected by regional trends and the daily drift of the main field, so it is the recommended method. A station spacing of 0.5 m, with similar spacing between lines, keeps at least 5 readings across the anomaly. Several things could make the real anomaly smaller: drum corrosion, wall thickness, which way the drum is lying, any remanent magnetisation (which could strengthen or weaken the signal), and nearby steel debris. The reported detection limit of 6-11 ft (about 1.8-3.4 m) means a drum at 3 m is near the edge of what has been found in practice, even though the model gives a strong signal. Because a sphere's anomaly falls off roughly with the cube of depth, a slightly deeper drum or a smaller effective susceptibility would drop the signal quickly. Treat the model as optimistic and run a test line over a known drum if you can.

I modelled the valley fill as a rectangular block (prism) 1000 m wide along the profile and 5000 m long across it, from 5 m to 60 m depth, with a density contrast of -100 kg/m³ for clay/till against shale. I used the tool's default magnetic susceptibility contrast for clay against shale, -0.0004 SI, with induced magnetisation only. I used a generic central Illinois location (40°N, 89°W, mid-2024) for the Earth's magnetic field. That should be close to the stated 51843 nT and 67° inclination, but the tool did not report the field it actually used. Gravity: the peak is a -221 µGal low against 11.2 µGal effective noise (S/N about 20), so the valley is clearly detectable. A 200 m spacing gives at least 5 stations across the roughly 1 km wide low. Use 50–100 m spacing near the valley edges to map the walls, and run profiles longer than the valley so the background level is well tied. You will need careful elevation surveying (about 3 µGal per cm), terrain corrections and removal of the regional trend, because real glacial fill varies in thickness and density. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 6.4 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 3.2), so it is only marginal. That result depends entirely on the assumed susceptibility contrast, and magnetic glacial debris and anything at the surface could swamp it. Gradiometer: the peak is about 0.38 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 0.74), so it is not detectable. A body this large and broad produces almost no vertical gradient. If the real density contrast is closer to -30 to -50 kg/m³, gravity would still give S/N above 5. Seismic refraction or reflection, or electrical resistivity, would help confirm the bedrock surface.

Results come from one forward-model run. The tank was modelled as a sphere of the same volume (about 10 m³, 2.7 m across) with its top at 1 m depth, in soil, with induced magnetisation only and an apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI. The model used a site location of 40°N, 89°W in Illinois. The main field it calculated for that point (taken as about 51,800 nT, 67° inclination) matches the field values you gave. Gravity: the tank was treated as an empty air-filled hole (-1920 kg/m³ against soil). That gives about -24 µGal against 11.2 µGal of noise, so S/N is 2.1, just inside the marginal range. The weight of the steel shell, or any fuel or water left inside, would shrink this anomaly and could make it undetectable. Magnetics: both magnetic methods give anomalies thousands of times larger than the noise (S/N about 4,900 for total field and about 17,000 for the gradient). Because the sphere model leaves out remanence and the tank's real shape, the actual amplitude and shape may be quite different, but detection is certain either way. With signals this large, the instruments may saturate or the sensor may lose lock right over the tank. Nearby steel or cultural noise such as pipes, fences, vehicles and buried scrap could also hide the tank or be mistaken for it. The gradiometer is the best choice: it removes daily field changes and picks out the shallow source more sharply. Use about 0.2 m between stations, with profile lines no more than 0.5 m apart. If you need to be sure it's a void rather than solid steel, a ground-penetrating radar or electromagnetic check would help.

Results come from one forward-model run. The pipe was modelled as a solid horizontal cylinder 0.6 m across, with its top 1.5 m down, lying at right angles to the survey line in soil. It was given an apparent susceptibility contrast of 2 SI and an air-filled density contrast of about -1920 kg/m3. Only induced magnetisation was included. The main field came from the model's field table for a site at about 54.5 N, 2 W in June 2024. I did not check it against the stated 49701 nT, inclination 68.3 degrees and declination 0.5 degrees, but a field that close should give a very similar answer. Gravity: the anomaly is about 4 microGal against 11.2 microGal of noise (S/N 0.36), so the pipe cannot be detected. The model suggested 0.5 m station spacing, but this is given as 0 under the survey rules. Total-field magnetics: about 773 nT against 2 nT of noise (S/N about 386), so it is clearly detectable at 0.2 m spacing. Gradiometer: about 580 nT against 0.51 nT of noise (S/N about 1137), so it is clearly detectable at 0.2 m spacing. The gradiometer is recommended because it suppresses regional and diurnal variation and gives the sharpest anomaly. Both magnetic signals are so large that cover depth, diameter or susceptibility could be off by a lot without changing the verdict. Real anomalies will differ because of remanent magnetisation in the steel, the pipe being hollow, cathodic protection, joints and welds, and nearby steel such as fences or vehicles. Gradiometer readings this large may saturate or clip the instrument's range, so check its range setting. Run survey lines at right angles to the expected route of the pipe.

I modelled the bomb as a sphere of equal volume, 0.68 m across, with its top 1.5 m deep (centre at about 1.84 m). I used induced magnetisation only, with an apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI and no remanence. Both magnetic sensors were set 2 m above the ground, with a 1 m gradiometer baseline. Gravity: the 'air in soil' material gives a density contrast of -1920 kg/m3. The peak is only about 0.6 µGal against 11.2 µGal of noise (S/N about 0.06), so gravity cannot detect it. A real steel casing filled with explosive would be denser than air, but the signal would still be far too small. Total-field magnetics: peak about 66 nT against 2 nT noise (S/N about 33), so it is clearly detectable. Gradiometer: peak about 33 nT against 0.51 nT noise (S/N about 66), the best result. The tool calculated the main field from the IGRF model at an approximate Latvian location (56.95 N, 24.1 E), which should be close to the field you gave (51,890 nT, inclination 71.7°). I took the 0.5 m station spacing from the tool. Hand calculation suggests the anomaly is about 3–4 m wide at half maximum at this sensor height, so 0.5 m sampling is plenty. Drone line spacing should also be 0.5–1 m. A remanent magnetisation, which is common in steel bomb casings, could change the shape and size of the anomaly considerably. The modelled amplitudes are therefore only indicative, and any confirmed target should be handled by an explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) team.

Results come from one run of the detectability model. The bomb was modelled as a sphere 0.68 m across with its top 3.7 m below the seabed, in sand, with an apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI. Because the casing is steel, the model assumed a 'material' of air, which gives a density contrast of -2000 kg/m3. Both magnetic sensors were set 4 m above the seabed. Gravity: the peak is about 0.13 µGal against about 11.2 µGal of noise (S/N 0.01), so it cannot detect the target and no station spacing is given. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 6.9 nT against 2.0 nT of noise (S/N 3.4), which is marginal. Gradiometer: the peak is about 2.0 nT against 0.51 nT of noise (S/N 4.0), which is also marginal but the better of the two, so it is the recommended method. Main field: the model took the main field from its built-in Earth-field model, using an assumed site at 54.5°N, 6.5°E on 2024-06-01. It was not given your stated values (50086 nT, inclination 68.8°, declination 3.4°). These should be close, but this was not checked, and any difference would change the magnetic peaks slightly. Station spacing: the 1 m spacing for both magnetic methods is the model's output, not a value I worked out. It is finer than the at-least-5-stations-across-the-anomaly rule needs at this depth, so use it as an upper limit and keep line spacing similar. Main uncertainties: the model includes only induced magnetisation. Remanence in the bomb, its shape and orientation, and a deeper burial (the 4 m case puts it about 8 m from the sensor) could lower the signal below detection. Seabed debris and motion noise in the towed system are not modelled. Flying lower (about 2 m or less above the seabed) would raise S/N sharply.

I modelled the shell as a 0.16 m diameter sphere with its top at 0.4 m, in soil. I used the given apparent susceptibility contrast of 3 SI and the density contrast of air in soil (-1920 kg/m³). Induced magnetisation only, no remanence. The main field came from the model for Central Spain (about 40°N, 4°W). It should be close to the given 45088 nT, inclination 55.1° and declination 0.6°. Gravity: the peak is about 0.12 µGal against 11.2 µGal of noise (S/N about 0.01), so a gravity survey cannot detect it. Total-field magnetics: the peak is about 36 nT with the sensor 0.5 m above ground, S/N about 18, so it is clearly detectable at about 0.2 m station spacing. Gradiometer: the peak is about 102 nT with the lower sensor 0.2 m above ground and a 1 m baseline, S/N about 200, so it is clearly detectable at about 0.1 m spacing. This is the method to use, as in F07. Treat these as best-case numbers: the shape is an ideal sphere in uniform ground with no remanence. Real shells may carry remanent magnetisation, lie at different angles and sit near other iron debris, which changes the anomaly's size and shape. Because the anomaly is so narrow, keep the walking traverses about 0.25 m or closer apart and the sensor height steady.

Modelled as a sphere 0.16 m across (equal volume to a 105 mm shell), top 0.4 m deep, with a susceptibility contrast of 3 SI. Gravity used the material tables (air in soil, about -1920 kg/m3); magnetics used induced magnetisation only, no remanence. The main field came from the tool's built-in model for Madrid (40.4N, 3.7W, date 2025-01-01). It was not set to the stated 45088 nT, 55.1 deg inclination and 0.6 deg declination, but should be close to those values. Gravity is about 0.1 microGal against 11 microGal of noise, so it cannot detect the target. Total-field magnetics gives about 2.3 nT against 2 nT of noise (S/N about 1.1), so it is not detectable with the sensor 2 m up. The gradiometer gives about 1.5 nT against 0.51 nT of noise (S/N about 2.9), which is marginal but the best option. The gradiometer spacing is 0.2 m, and line spacing should be about the same. Lowering the drone or using a ground cart (sensor about 0.2-0.5 m above ground) would raise the signal sharply and make the target clearly detectable. Treating the steel shell as having an apparent susceptibility of 3 is a simplification. Remanence, the shell's elongated shape and its orientation could change the anomaly a lot, and so could magnetic soil noise or nearby ferrous debris. Follow the usual UXO safety procedures.

Modelled as a 0.4 m sphere (same volume as the bomb) with its top at 3 m. Results: gravity S/N about 0.004, total-field magnetics S/N about 6.8, gradiometer S/N about 19. The main field was taken from the tool's model for about 51°N, 10.5°E in 2020. It should be close to the given 49490 nT, inclination 66.7° and declination 4.1°, but these exact values were not entered. Gravity used the air-in-soil density contrast (-1920 kg/m³) because that material was specified. A real steel bomb has a positive density contrast, but its anomaly would still be far below the 11 µGal noise, so gravity is not a practical method. Gravity was not detectable, so its spacing is given as 0; the tool's 0.5 m spacing for gravity does not apply. The magnetic results assume induced magnetisation only, using an apparent susceptibility of 3 SI to stand in for the bomb's shape and demagnetisation effects. Remanence, which steel ordnance often carries, could make the anomaly much larger or smaller and change its shape. Total-field magnetics is only just above the clear-detection threshold of S/N 5, so a smaller or deeper bomb, or more magnetic noise from soil, scrap or infrastructure, could make it marginal. The gradiometer has a good safety margin at 3 m. A spacing of 0.5 m or less, applied to both line spacing and along-line sampling, is recommended for finding UXO. In practice, follow up any picks with borehole magnetometer probes.
